correctness.rationale: For a unit vector and a fixed partition, write \(x,y\) for the two selected energy pieces and \(u,v\) for their complementary dual pieces. Dual reconstruction gives \(1\le\sqrt{xu}+\sqrt{yv}\), while the Bessel bounds give \(u\le B_\Gamma-y\) and \(v\le B_\Lambda-x\). Cauchy--Schwarz therefore yields \(1\le\sqrt{E(S-E)}\), where \(E=x+y\), forcing \(E\ge(S-\sqrt{S^2-4})/2\). For sharpness, choose two real coefficient vectors \(\lambda,\gamma\) with squared norms \(B_\Lambda,B_\Gamma\) and dot product one. The symmetric matrix \(\lambda\lambda^{\mathsf T}+(J\gamma)(J\gamma)^{\mathsf T}\) has trace \(S\) and determinant one; rotating to an eigenbasis makes a mixed weaving attain its smaller eigenvalue, exactly \(A_*\). This also verifies admissibility requires \(B_\Lambda B_\Gamma\ge1\).

The earlier generalized-frame paper proves weaving and studies optimal bounds abstractly but no checked source provides the sharp Bessel-only root formula or its all-parameter one-dimensional extremizers. The 2025 operator-valued-frame abstract is a serious plausible-overlap source because it mentions optimal universal bounds and dual weaving; however its theorem text was inaccessible under the available authorized session, so it cannot be asserted to cover this specific Bessel-only optimization. Under the owner rule, that access limitation is retained as a residual risk rather than converted into failure.

value.rationale: The known explicit Bessel-only bound is materially weaker. Determining the exact best lower weaving constant from only the two Bessel resources, and proving sharpness for every feasible pair with a minimal extremizer, is a natural optimization result in dual-frame weaving rather than a cosmetic constant improvement.

final_claim: If \(\Lambda\) and \(\Gamma\) are dual g-frames with Bessel upper bounds \(B_\Lambda\) and \(B_\Gamma\), then every weaving has lower bound at least \(A_*=(S-\sqrt{S^2-4})/2\), \(S=B_\Lambda+B_\Gamma\); this constant is best possible using only the two Bessel bounds, for every admissible pair of bounds.
limitations: The theorem uses only the two Bessel upper bounds and duality; additional frame geometry may improve the lower bound.
Sharpness is already attained by a real one-dimensional two-index dual pair.
